ru: я уже (сделал) — сокращение от I have
type: have — a subject plus the auxiliary *have*
register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
contrast: *'ve* contracts the auxiliary only. American English does not contract *have* meaning 'own': *I have a car*, never ✗ *I've a car* (that is British and dated). And no contraction can end a clause: *Yes, I have*, never ✗ *Yes, I've*.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *I have*, the auxiliary of the present perfect.
examples: *I've* lived in Chicago since 2015.
*I've* already eaten, thanks.
*I've* got to leave by six.

ru: ты/вы уже (сделал) — сокращение от you have
type: have — a subject plus the auxiliary *have*
register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
contrast: Unstressed, *you've* is said /jəv/ and the *'ve* is easy to miss: *You've seen it* and *You saw it* differ by one weak syllable. The written trap is the pronoun — *you've* is *you have*, *you're* is *you are*, and *your* is the possessive.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *you have*, the auxiliary of the present perfect.
examples: *You've* been working too hard lately.
*You've* got mail.
If *you've* finished the form, bring it to the window.

ru: мы уже (сделали) — сокращение от we have
type: have — a subject plus the auxiliary *have*
register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
contrast: *We've* is pronounced exactly like *weave*. Do not confuse it with *we'd* (*we would* or *we had*) or *we're* (*we are*).

senses.gloss: The contraction of *we have*, the auxiliary of the present perfect.
examples: *We've* known each other since college.
*We've* got a problem with the heater.
*We've* never been to Texas.

ru: они уже (сделали) — сокращение от they have
type: have — a subject plus the auxiliary *have*
register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
contrast: The three *they* contractions are different words: *they're* is *they are*, *they'd* is *they would* or *they had*, and *they've* is *they have*. None of them is *their*.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *they have*, the auxiliary of the present perfect.
examples: *They've* lived in that house for thirty years.
*They've* already left for the airport.
I don't think *they've* met before.

ru: которые уже (сделали) — сокращение от who have
type: have — the relative or question word *who* plus the auxiliary *have*
register: standard — but far rarer than *who's*, and mostly heard rather than written
question: *Who've you told?* is normal in speech; in writing most Americans spell it out — *Who have you told?*
contrast: *Who've* is *who have*; *who's* is *who is* or *who has*; *whose* is the possessive and takes no apostrophe.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *who have*.
examples: Students *who've* missed three classes can't take the final.
There are plenty of people *who've* never heard of him.
*Who've* you been talking to?

ru: мог бы (тогда) — сокращение от could have
type: modal — *could* plus a contracted *have*
register: informal — normal in speech; formal writing spells it out as *could have*
question: There is no contracted question: *Could you have known?*, never ✗ *Could've you known?*
contrast: The *-'ve* is unstressed /əv/ and sounds exactly like *of*, which is why ✗ *could of* is the most common spelling error in written American English. It is never correct, in any register — if you cannot hear which it is, expand it to *could have*.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *could have*: what was possible but did not happen.
senses.ru: мог бы (тогда), мог и не сделать
examples: You *could've* told me you were bringing someone.
The whole thing *could've* been avoided.
I *could've* sworn I left my keys on the table.

ru: сделал бы (тогда) — сокращение от would have
type: modal — *would* plus a contracted *have*
register: informal — normal in speech; formal writing spells it out as *would have*
question: There is no contracted question: *Would you have come?*, never ✗ *Would've you come?*
contrast: ✗ *would of* is never correct — the *-'ve* is unstressed /əv/ and only sounds like *of*. Watch the halves of the third conditional: *If I'd known, I would've called* — *had* in the *if* clause, *would have* in the main clause, never ✗ *If I would've known*.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *would have*: what was going to be true but was not.
examples: I *would've* called, but my phone was dead.
She *would've* made a great teacher.
Nobody *would've* guessed he was nervous.

ru: надо было (сделать) — сокращение от should have
type: modal — *should* plus a contracted *have*
register: informal — normal in speech; formal writing spells it out as *should have*
question: There is no contracted question: *Should I have said something?*, never ✗ *Should've I said something?*
contrast: ✗ *should of* is never correct, however much the *-'ve* sounds like *of*. Note what the form means: *should've* is always a reproach or a regret about the past — *You should've called* says that you did not call.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *should have*: what was the right thing to do and was not done.
examples: I *should've* studied more for that test.
You *should've* seen the look on his face.
We *should've* left an hour ago.

ru: возможно, сделал — сокращение от might have
type: modal — *might* plus a contracted *have*
register: informal — normal in speech; formal writing spells it out as *might have*
contrast: ✗ *might of* is never correct. Keep the two deductions apart: *might've* is a guess (*He might've left* — maybe, maybe not), while *must've* is a conclusion (*He must've left* — I am sure of it).

senses.gloss: The contraction of *might have*: a guess about the past, or about what nearly happened.
senses.ru: возможно, сделал; мог бы и сделать
examples: He *might've* left already — his car is gone.
I *might've* put it in the other drawer.
You *might've* warned me before I signed it.

ru: наверняка сделал — сокращение от must have
type: modal — *must* plus a contracted *have*
register: informal — normal in speech; formal writing spells it out as *must have*
contrast: ✗ *must of* is never correct. And *must've* is never obligation in the past: *He must've left* means 'I am sure he left'; for obligation you say *he had to leave*.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *must have*: a confident conclusion about the past.
examples: He *must've* left — the lights are off.
You *must've* been exhausted after that drive.
I *must've* missed the turn somewhere.

ru: я бы; я уже — сокращение от I would или I had
type: would — or *had*; the verb that follows tells you which
register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
ambiguity: *I'd* is *I would* before a bare verb (*I'd go*) and *I had* before a past participle (*I'd gone*). Two fixed phrases settle it by themselves: *I'd better* is always *had*, *I'd rather* is always *would*.
contrast: The third conditional uses both in one sentence: *If I'd known, I'd have said something* — the first *I'd* is *had*, the second is *would*.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *I would*.
examples: *I'd* love to come to the party.
*I'd* rather stay home tonight.
If I had the money, *I'd* buy it.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *I had*, the auxiliary of the past perfect.
examples: By the time she called, *I'd* already gone to bed.
*I'd* never seen snow before that winter.
*I'd* better get going.

ru: ты бы; ты уже — сокращение от you would или you had
type: would — or *had*; the verb that follows tells you which
register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
ambiguity: *You'd like it* is *would*; *You'd finished* is *had*. *You'd better* is *had* — and in speech it shrinks further, to *you better* or even a bare *better*.
contrast: *You'd* is *you would* or *you had*, never *you are* — that is *you're*.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *you would*.
examples: *You'd* like her — everybody does.
*You'd* be surprised how often that happens.
If you asked him, *you'd* get the same answer.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *you had*, the auxiliary of the past perfect.
examples: *You'd* better call your mother.
She said *you'd* already paid for the tickets.
By then *you'd* been waiting almost an hour.

ru: он бы; он уже — сокращение от he would или he had
type: would — or *had*; the verb that follows tells you which
register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
ambiguity: *He'd go* is *would*; *He'd gone* is *had*. *He'd better* is *had*, *he'd rather* is *would*.
contrast: *He'd* is a homophone of *heed*, and in the middle of a sentence the *h* often drops, so *what he'd said* runs together as one word. Do not confuse it with *he's*, which is *he is* or *he has*.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *he would*.
examples: *He'd* never admit it, but he was scared.
I asked if *he'd* help us move.
*He'd* rather walk than wait for the bus.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *he had*, the auxiliary of the past perfect.
examples: By the time we got there, *he'd* eaten.
She told me *he'd* been sick all week.
*He'd* better have a good excuse.

ru: она бы; она уже — сокращение от she would или she had
type: would — or *had*; the verb that follows tells you which
register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
ambiguity: *She'd like it* is *would*; *She'd liked it* is *had*. The participle is the whole test: *she'd take it* (would) against *she'd taken it* (had).
contrast: *She'd* is *she would* or *she had*, never *she is* or *she has* — those are *she's*.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *she would*.
examples: *She'd* like to meet you sometime.
*She'd* rather not talk about it.
I knew *she'd* say no.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *she had*, the auxiliary of the past perfect.
examples: *She'd* already left when I got there.
*She'd* never flown before that trip.
He mentioned that *she'd* been promoted twice.

ru: это было бы; это уже — сокращение от it would или it had
type: would — or *had*, though the *had* reading is rare
register: informal — common in speech, seldom written outside dialogue; in print, spell out *it would*
ambiguity: *It'd take an hour* is *would*; *It'd rained all night* is *had*. With *it*, the *would* reading is far commoner.
contrast: Unlike the one-syllable *it's*, *it'd* has two syllables, and the American flapped *t* makes it sound close to 'id-ud'. It is a spoken form: write *it would*.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *it would*.
examples: *It'd* be great if you could come.
*It'd* take about two hours to drive there.
I thought *it'd* be colder than this.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *it had*, the auxiliary of the past perfect.
examples: The ground was soaked — *it'd* rained all night.
By morning *it'd* stopped snowing.

ru: мы бы; мы уже — сокращение от we would или we had
type: would — or *had*; the verb that follows tells you which
register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
ambiguity: *We'd go* is *would*; *We'd gone* is *had*. *We'd better* is *had*, *we'd rather* is *would*.
contrast: *We'd* sounds exactly like *weed*. Keep it apart from *we've* (*we have*) and *we're* (*we are*).

senses.gloss: The contraction of *we would*.
examples: *We'd* love to have you over for dinner.
*We'd* rather leave before the traffic starts.
If it were cheaper, *we'd* buy it.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *we had*, the auxiliary of the past perfect.
examples: *We'd* already eaten by the time she showed up.
They told us *we'd* missed the deadline.
*We'd* better hurry.

ru: они бы; они уже — сокращение от they would или they had
type: would — or *had*; the verb that follows tells you which
register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
ambiguity: *They'd agree* is *would*; *They'd agreed* is *had* — and here the two differ by one consonant, so listen for the *-ed*.
contrast: *They'd* is *they would* or *they had*; *they've* is *they have*; *they're* is *they are*; *their* and *there* are not contractions at all.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *they would*.
examples: *They'd* never agree to that.
I figured *they'd* call back by now.
*They'd* rather pay cash.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *they had*, the auxiliary of the past perfect.
examples: *They'd* already sold the house when we called.
She said *they'd* been friends since high school.

ru: было бы; уже было — сокращение от there would или there had
type: would — or *had*; with the existential *there*
register: standard — much commoner in speech than in writing
ambiguity: *There'd be trouble* is *would*; *There'd been trouble* is *had*. After *there*, the *had* reading is always followed by *been*.
contrast: This is the existential *there* of *there is* and *there was*, not the place word — and never *their* or *they're*.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *there would*.
examples: *There'd* be a lot less traffic if we left at six.
Nobody warned us *there'd* be a fee.
If we canceled now, *there'd* be no refund.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *there had*, always before *been*.
examples: *There'd* been a fire in the building the week before.
She had no idea *there'd* been any complaints.

ru: кто бы; который уже — сокращение от who would или who had
type: would — or *had*; the verb that follows tells you which
register: standard — normal in speech and in ordinary writing
ambiguity: *Who'd want that?* is *would*; *the man who'd left* is *had*. Casual speech adds a third reading that is never written outside dialogue: *Who'd you call?* is *who did*.
contrast: *Who'd* is a homophone of *hood*. It is not *who's* (*who is* or *who has*), and not *whose*, the possessive, which takes no apostrophe.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *who would*.
examples: *Who'd* have thought it would end like that?
*Who'd* want to drive four hours for one meeting?

senses.gloss: The contraction of *who had*, the auxiliary of the past perfect.
examples: The witness *who'd* seen the car never came forward.
He introduced me to a cousin *who'd* just moved to town.

ru: это было бы — сокращение от that would или that had
type: would — or *had*, though the *had* reading is rare
register: informal — speech and dialogue only; in writing, spell out *that would*
ambiguity: *That'd be great* is *would*; *that'd been settled* is *had*. With *that*, *'d* is almost always *would*.
contrast: Two syllables, with the American flapped *t*, so it sounds close to 'thad-ud'. It is not *that's*, which is *that is* or *that has*.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *that would*.
examples: *That'd* be great, thanks.
*That'd* cost more than the car is worth.
I didn't think *that'd* work.

senses.gloss: The contraction of *that had*, the auxiliary of the past perfect.
examples: He said *that'd* already been decided.
We assumed *that'd* been taken care of.
